title: Eat this scroll (Ezekiel 3:1–3)
hook: the prophet eats a scroll and it is "as honey for sweetness"

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the river Chebar, the heavens opened over the exiles, and Ezekiel saw the merkavah, a throne with wheels. Your line was God in exile too. Where did you look up? Today, the vision gives him something to eat. Day eight hundred ten.

"Open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee." That's what Ezekiel hears, right after the vision. A hand reaches toward him, holding a scroll. It's unrolled before him, and it's written on both sides, front and back. And the text tells us what's written there: lamentations, and mourning, and woe. A scroll of bad news, inside and out. Not a scroll to read aloud, or to file away, or to hand to someone else. He is told to eat it.
screen: `A HAND HOLDING A SCROLL.` → `WRITTEN FRONT AND BACK.` → `LAMENTATIONS, MOURNING, WOE.`

segments.voice: Here is how the text tells it, in the King James words: "Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." Stop on that. The words on the scroll are grief. The taste is honey. Ezekiel doesn't say the message changed. It's still lamentation and woe; the rest of his book will be full of hard news. What changes is that it's no longer outside him. He's swallowed it. It's in him now, and the word of God, even when it's heavy, tastes sweet in his mouth. Notice the order too. Before he speaks a single word to the exiles, he takes the words in. He doesn't read them off the page to the crowd. He eats them first. And then he's told: go, get thee unto the house of Israel, and speak with my words unto them. The book of Psalms has a line that sits close to this one: the judgments of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. And Jewish life has a custom that makes the picture real. In some communities, on a child's first day of learning Hebrew letters, honey is put on the letters, or on a slate, and the child licks it off. The idea is simple: learning should taste sweet. The scroll Ezekiel eats isn't a children's lesson. It's hard. But the image holds both: words you take all the way in, even difficult ones, can become part of you, and that can be sweet.
screen: `OPEN THY MOUTH, AND EAT.` · then, large: `AS HONEY FOR SWEETNESS.` · then: `TAKE THE WORDS IN FIRST.` · `HONEY ON THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: savor one sentence. Pick one line you've read recently, from scripture, a book, a letter, even a sign. If nothing comes, use Ezekiel's: it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness. Settle, and breathe. Say the line once, slowly, under your breath. Then again, slower. Let each word sit before you move to the next, the way you'd hold something sweet in your mouth instead of swallowing it fast. Notice which word has the most taste. If you pray, you can let that line become your prayer for now. The bell holds the time.
Eat this scroll. Ezekiel is told to eat a scroll of lamentation and woe, and it tastes as honey for sweetness. Today's word.
Your line: sweet as honey. Today, read one sentence twice as slowly as you normally would, and notice what it tastes like the second time. Day eight hundred ten.

howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 2–3 as the prophet's call, and some communities mark a child's first lesson in Hebrew letters with honey so that learning tastes sweet.

fork.setup: you're Ezekiel. a hand holds out a scroll of mourning and woe and tells you to eat it. what happens?
options: it tastes as honey for sweetness.
fork.reveal: he eats it, and it is in his mouth as honey for sweetness, even though the words are grief.

original.note: Hebrew: honey, the taste of the scroll in Ezekiel's mouth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange story about a man eating paper.
what it means: the prophet takes the words all the way in before he speaks them.
what a scholar hears: a message of woe tastes as honey, and the image sits beside the psalm line that God's judgments are sweeter than honey.
